{{Short description|Norwegian entrepreneur (born 1937)}}
[[File:1967 ralph Høibakk Small.jpg|thumb|Ralph Høibakk in 1967]]
'''Ralph Høibakk''' (born 14 July 1937) is a [[Norway|Norwegian]] entrepreneur. He established the [[Tandberg Data]] company in 1978, which produced ergonomically designed laptops and keyboards. Høibakk left the company in 1986, and started Høibakk Invest, which provides [[management consulting]] for new enterprises. He is also a mountaineer, and has climbed the [[Tirich Mir]], [[Mount Everest]] and [[Drangnag Ri]] mountains in Asia with Norwegian philosopher [[Arne Næss]] and [[Arne Næss Jr.]]

Høibakk obtained a [[PhD]] in mathematics in 2017 (age 79) at the [[University of Tromsø]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://uit.no/nyheter/artikkel?p_document_id=519527&p_dim=210108|title=Ralph (79 år ung) fikk sin doktorgrad|last=Viklem|first=Eidum, Espen|date=19 May 2017|website=University of Tromsø|language=no|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=18 April 2020}}</ref>

== Early and personal life ==
Høibakk was born to the engineer Rolf Høibakk (1908–2002) and his wife Mary Wilthil. In 1965, Høibakk married Inger Holm, but divorced her in 1998.<ref name=nbl/>

==Career==
Høibakk grew up at [[Rjukan]] and took [[examen artium]] in 1956. After that, he studied at the [[Norwegian Institute of Technology]] until 1962. He then served his [[conscription]] at the [[Norwegian Defence Research Establishment]] at [[Kjeller]]. During his conscription, he became familiar with the [[Manchester computers|Manchester computer]] named FREDERIC, which was imported from the [[University of Manchester]].<ref name=nbl/>

From 1963 to 1965, Høibakk worked at the [[SINTEF]] research centre in [[Trondheim]]. After he left SINTEF, Høibakk was appointed [[managing director]] of the computer technology company Nor-Data, which he remained for 13 years. In 1978, he was appointed chairman of [[Tandberg#Tandbergs Radiofabrikk|Tandberg Radio]]{{'s}} data division. In the same year the [[Ministry of Trade and Industry (Norway)|Norwegian Ministry of Trade and Industry]] decided to bankrupt Tandberg Radio, which was the first time the Norwegian government had decided to bankrupt a company. Høibakk decided to start a new company, [[Tandberg Data]]. It gained surplus in the first years, and in 1978 it released its first product; a table computer. In the following years, Tandberg Data produced [[Keyboard (computing)|keyboards]] and [[personal computer]]s which were ergonomically designed.<ref name=nbl>{{cite encyclopedia|year=2001|title=Ralph Høibakk|encyclopedia=[[Norsk biografisk leksikon]]|first=Arild|last=Haraldsen|editor=Helle, Knut|editor-link=Knut Helle|publisher=Kunnskapsforlaget|location=Oslo|url=https://www.snl.no/.nbl_biografi/Ralph_H%C3%B8ibakk/utdypning|language=Norwegian|access-date=20 March 2011}}</ref>

In the 1980s, Tandberg Data tried to start business in the [[United States]], but without success.<ref name=nbl/> In 1986, Høibakk resigned from his position in the company, and established Høibakk Invest AS, where he was the managing director.<ref>{{cite news|title=Ralph Høibakk 70 år|newspaper=[[Stavanger Aftenblad]]|date=14 July 2007|agency=[[Norwegian News Agency]]|page=12|language=Norwegian}}</ref> In 2000, he was appointed [[Professor#Norway|Professor II]] at the [[Narvik University College]].<ref name=nbl/>

== Mountaineering ==
Høibakk is a noted mountaineer. In 1958, he was part of the first climbing of [[Trollryggen]].<ref name=aftpost/> He also climbed the mountain [[Tirich Mir]] in an expedition led by the Norwegian philosopher [[Arne Næss]] in 1964.<ref name=aftpost>{{cite news|last=Jelstad|first=Jørgen|title=Med verden for sine føtter|url=http://www.aftenposten.no/reise/spesial/article2390811.ece|access-date=20 March 2011|newspaper=[[Aftenposten]]|date=26 April 2008|language=Norwegian}}</ref> In 1985, Høibakk climbed the [[Mount Everest]] with a group of 25 Norwegians, led by [[Arne Næss Jr.]]<ref>{{cite news|last=Strømmen|first=Karl R.|title="The Happiest Ever"|newspaper=[[Dagens Næringsliv]]|date=21 April 2010|page=64|language=Norwegian}}</ref> Ten years later, Høibakk climbed the Drangnag Ri mountain in Tibet with [[Chris Bonington]] and Bjørn Myhrer Lund. Høibakk and Bonington were hit by lightning at {{convert|6800|m}} above sea level.<ref name=aftpost/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Bonington|first=Chris|title=Drangnag-Ri|journal=The Alpine Journal|year=1996|pages=77–82|access-date=20 March 2011|author-link=Chris Bonington|url=https://www.alpinejournal.org.uk/Contents/Contents_1996_files/AJ%201996%2077-82%20Bonington%20Drangnag-Ri.pdf}}</ref> In 1990, Høibakk skied to the [[South Pole]] with a group of Norwegians who were the first Norwegians to reach the South Pole on ski since [[Roald Amundsen]].<ref name=nbl/> He later recalled that he found the ski trip a "bit boring".<ref name=aftpost/>
